fields.title: The Product Side of Recovery
fields.keyTakeaway: Data recovery creates discrepancies with external systems, and a reconciliation procedure with a "disputed issues resolved in favor of the user" rule must be prepared in advance, not during an outage.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Data is restored to a state from an hour ago. What do users see and what do we tell them?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A technically successful recovery can be a product disaster if the lost hour contained orders people paid for. Handling such situations takes weeks of support work — and this is work that can be planned in advance.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Restoring to a point in the past creates three classes of problems.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Disappeared actions.** Orders placed during the lost hour do not exist. But money was charged, emails sent, stores notified. External systems remember things we do not have.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Discrepancy with external systems.** The payment provider knows about payments, delivery services about orders. Reconciliation after recovery is mandatory and must be prepared in advance.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Repeated actions.** A user whose order disappeared will place it again. If reconciliation later restores the first one — you get two.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: *External system reconciliation procedure.* A script that compares our data with the provider and finds discrepancies. *Communication template.* What to write to people whose actions were lost. *Conflict resolution rule.* In favor of the user — always. Restored and repeated orders are sorted out manually, money is refunded immediately.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: A separate product decision — **what to do with partially lost state.** An order exists, but bonuses for it were not credited. It is easier to credit them again to everyone in the recovery window than to figure it out: the cost of an error in the user's favor is lower than the cost of investigation.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: The "post-recovery" procedure is written in advance, before it is needed.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/0: Reconciliation with the payment provider over the recovery window — all payments lacking an order.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/1: Reconciliation with the delivery service — all deliveries without an order.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/2: Restoring orders using provider data where possible.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/4: A personal email to everyone affected.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/5: Bonus compensation to everyone in the window.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Item 4 was discussed the longest. Agreed: refunds without investigation are cheaper than manual investigation, and much cheaper than dissatisfaction. For a one-hour window, this is a maximum of 800 orders, of which disputed ones are a handful.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Tested in a drill: provider reconciliation worked, delivery service reconciliation did not, because their API did not return deliveries for an arbitrary period. Discovered in a drill, not an outage.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Some actions are impossible to restore by definition: views, searches, drafts. Here the only answer is to acknowledge and not try.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Data recovery creates discrepancies with external systems, and a reconciliation procedure with a "disputed issues resolved in favor of the user" rule must be prepared in advance, not during an outage.
